meta.title: Who really said "Common Sense Is Nothing More Than a Deposit of Prejudices Laid Down in the Mind Before Age Eighteen"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Einstein’s idea, in Lincoln Barnett’s words. Barnett wrote it in Harper’s in 1948 — and Einstein wrote the book’s foreword.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Common Sense Is Nothing More Than a Deposit of Prejudices Laid Down in the Mind Before Age Eighteen'?
meta.ogDescription: Not a transcript. Lincoln Barnett ascribed the thought to Einstein in 1948 without quoting him — and Einstein wrote the foreword.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: This is a genuine grey area, and the honest answer is “his idea, someone else’s sentence”. The words first appear in the science writer Lincoln Barnett’s Harper’s Magazine article of May 1948: “But as Einstein has pointed out, common sense is actually nothing more than a deposit of prejudices laid down in the mind prior to the age of eighteen” — ascribed to Einstein, but deliberately not in quotation marks. Einstein then wrote the foreword to the book that article became, and raised no objection. No source in Einstein’s own words has ever been located.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The Universe and Dr. Einstein, Part II
Lincoln Barnett, in Harper’s Magazine, vol. 196, May 1948 — article begins p. 465, passage on p. 473, col. 1 (Quote Investigator verified this on microfilm)
The Universe and Dr. Einstein (London: Victor Gollancz, 1949; copyright 1948), passage on page 49 — with a foreword by Albert Einstein
Barnett used no quotation marks. The first appearance as a direct quotation is E. T. Bell’s Mathematics: Queen and Servant of Science (1951), p. 42.

source.excerpt: At first meeting, these facts are difficult to digest, but that is simply because classical physics assumed, unjustifiably, that an object preserves the same dimensions whether it is in motion or at rest and that a clock keeps the same rhythm in motion and at rest. Common sense dictates that this must be so. But as Einstein has pointed out, common sense is actually nothing more than a deposit of prejudices laid down in the mind prior to the age of eighteen. Every new idea one encounters in later years must combat this accretion of “self-evident” concepts.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ locates the earliest evidence in Lincoln Barnett’s “The Universe and Dr. Einstein: Part II”, Harper’s Magazine vol. 196, May 1948, page 473 — verified on microfilm — and records that Barnett did not place the words in quotation marks.

We then checked the book ourselves rather than taking the locator on trust. The Internet Archive’s text of the Victor Gollancz printing ↗ carries the sentence on the page numbered 49, in exactly the wording Quote Investigator reports, and Einstein’s own foreword — “Lincoln Barnett’s book represents a valuable contribution to popular scientific writing” — stands at the front of the same volume.

The first version in quotation marks is later and second-hand: E. T. Bell, Mathematics: Queen and Servant of Science (McGraw-Hill, 1951), chapter 3, page 42, recalling “Einstein’s remark that ‘common sense is nothing more than a deposit of prejudices laid down in the mind before you reach eighteen’”. See the 1951 citation ↗

Wikiquote files the line under “Disputed” for Einstein ↗, noting that Alice Calaprice’s The Ultimate Quotable Einstein calls it “probably not by Einstein” while pointing to the Barnett passage as a reasonably plausible source. We agree with that balance, which is why this page says “attributed” rather than “verified”.
source.excerptNote: Note what is not there: quotation marks. Barnett is summarising a position he attributes to Einstein, not transcribing him. We read this passage ourselves in the text of the Gollancz printing held by the Internet Archive ↗, on the page numbered 49, and it matches Quote Investigator’s transcription from the May 1948 Harper’s original word for word.

source.rightsNote: The wording everyone quotes is Lincoln Barnett’s, first published in Harper’s Magazine in May 1948 and in book form the same year — long after the pre-1931 cut-off for the US public domain, so this text is in copyright. Because no sentence in Einstein’s own words matching this line has been found, there is no separate Einstein source whose rights could be assessed.

author.name: Albert Einstein
author.heading: About Albert Einstein
author.bio: Anything wry and clever about school, imagination or stupidity tends to drift onto Einstein’s name; Wikiquote keeps unusually long Disputed and Misattributed lists for him precisely because, as it says itself, misattributed quotations for Einstein are very common. This line is a rarer and more interesting case: not a fabrication pinned on him after his death, but a view a working journalist ascribed to him in print while he was alive to read it, in a book he supplied a foreword for. That is a good deal more evidence than most Einstein quotations carry, and still short of proof he ever said it.

misattribution.heading: The fine print
misattribution.intro: Nobody is being framed here. The question is subtler: are these Einstein’s words, or Einstein’s idea in somebody else’s words?

items.why: Barnett wrote it. He attributed the view to Einstein and pointedly declined to use quotation marks, which is what a careful writer does when reporting a position rather than a sentence. Everything since is people quoting Barnett quoting Einstein. See the 1948 passage ↗

items.scope: First put in quotation marks by
items.why: In Mathematics: Queen and Servant of Science (1951), page 42, Bell recalled “Einstein’s remark” and set it inside quotation marks for the first time — three years after Barnett, and from memory. Compare the two ↗

items.who: “Common sense is the collection of prejudices acquired by age eighteen”
items.why: That is the tightened version most sites print. Alice Calaprice files it at page 481 of The Ultimate Quotable Einstein (2010) under “Probably Not By Einstein”, having found no supporting citation for it. See the 2010 entry ↗
Wikiquote keeps the line under Disputed ↗, citing Calaprice’s doubt alongside the Barnett passage as a plausible origin — the same split verdict this page reaches.

misattribution.truthLine: Best evidence: the sentence people quote is Lincoln Barnett’s, from Harper’s Magazine, May 1948, page 473 — a view he ascribed to Einstein without claiming to quote him. Einstein wrote the foreword to the resulting book — evidence, as Quote Investigator puts it, that he had read the manuscript and had not objected. That is real evidence. It is still not a transcript.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Barnett was not making an aphorism; he was making an argument. The paragraph is about why relativity feels absurd — why a moving clock keeping a different rhythm offends us — and the common-sense line is the hinge. His point was that the intuitions physics has to overturn are not innate truths but habits, laid down early and defended fiercely. Einstein’s gift, Barnett went on, was an unwillingness to accept any unproven principle as self-evident.

Detached from that paragraph, the sentence became something else: a general-purpose licence to distrust received opinion, printed on posters and pinned to Einstein because he is the shorthand for genius. The idea survived the journey. The argument it belonged to did not.
detailsBody: The strongest evidence for Einstein is the foreword. He wrote it for the book that carries this passage, and it is warm: the work is “a valuable contribution to popular scientific writing” and “the main ideas of the theory of relativity are extremely well presented”. That tells us he read the manuscript, or enough of it to endorse it, and did not ask for the line to come out. But be precise about what it proves: the foreword praises the book in general and never mentions this sentence. It is evidence of no objection, not evidence of authorship.

The evidence on the other side is the compact version everybody actually shares. Alice Calaprice, who edited the standard collection of Einstein quotations for Princeton, puts “common sense is the collection of prejudices acquired by age eighteen” in her “Probably Not By Einstein” section, because no citation supports it. Both things can be true at once: the thought is fairly attributed to Einstein, and the crisp sentence attached to his name was written by other people.

sourcesVerified.claim: Earliest evidence is Lincoln Barnett, "The Universe and Dr. Einstein: Part II", Harper's Magazine vol. 196, May 1948, start p. 465, quote p. 473, col. 1, verified on microfilm; Barnett did not use quotation marks.
The book edition (Victor Gollancz, London, 1949, copyright 1948) carries the passage at p. 49 and a foreword by Albert Einstein dated 10 September 1948, quote p. 6.
E. T. Bell, Mathematics: Queen and Servant of Science (McGraw-Hill, 1951), ch. 3, p. 42, is the first instance placing the words in quotation marks.
The Ultimate Quotable Einstein (ed. Alice Calaprice, Princeton, 2010) lists the short form at p. 481 under "Probably Not By Einstein" with no supporting citation.

The scanned text of the Gollancz printing carries the sentence on the page numbered 49, in the wording QI reports, and Einstein's foreword ("Lincoln Barnett's book represents a valuable contribution to popular scientific writing") at the front. Read directly.
Wikiquote lists this line in its Disputed section for Einstein, citing both Calaprice's "probably not by Einstein" and the Barnett passage as a reasonably plausible source.
Lincoln Kinnear Barnett (1909-1979) was an American editor and author.
Albert Einstein lived 1879 to 1955 and was a German-born theoretical physicist.
